question: The report was replaced and Pauline's name was on it. What does the scenario establish about what happened?

options.text: It's never established — both readings stay possible and he has no way to resolve it
options.note: This is the chapter's whole design. If you finished it still wondering, that isn't the writing failing. That's the experience.

options.text: Not knowing is itself part of the harm, separately from whatever happened
options.note: He can't be angry, because there may be nothing to be angry at. He can't let it go, because there may be. That costs him all afternoon.

options.text: The conclusion about him got reached without anyone checking
options.note: One file, modified 09:52. The version history was one click away and nobody opened it — including the person who decided what it meant.

options.text: Pauline deliberately stole the work to get ahead
options.note: The game never says so, and her account holds up. Deciding she's a thief makes this one woman's vendetta rather than a pattern — which is exactly the reading the chapter refuses.

options.text: It was a technical fault in the shared drive
options.note: Also never established. Reaching for the innocent explanation is the same mistake as reaching for the malicious one: both let you stop thinking about it.

options.text: He should have kept his own copy or worked outside the shared drive
options.note: A sensible habit that only he needs. Note it's offered afterwards, as though the gap were his.

question: Mahalia's "you clean up so well" is delivered as a compliment. Why is it still a problem?

options.text: It rewards him for work outside his role that he was singled out to do
options.note: He was the last one near the kitchenette, and that was enough. Praise for it closes the loop: the task was his, and he was good at it, so it stays his.

options.text: It frames domestic competence as his contribution on a day he did the report twice
options.note: Nobody complimented the report. Two people said it was good in the meeting, and this is the line he takes home.

options.text: The second meaning lands on his appearance whether or not it was intended
options.note: It works twice and he has to decide, in the moment, which one to hear. Meaning it kindly doesn't spare him that.

options.text: She used an unprofessional tone of voice
options.note: Her tone was warm. That's what makes it hard to point at, and it's why he says nothing.

options.text: She should have offered to help him clean
options.note: It would have been nice. It also leaves intact the bit that matters — that he was the one asked.

options.text: It was said in front of other colleagues
options.note: An audience makes it stick. Said in an empty kitchen it would carry exactly the same message.

question: His answer in the #platform-eng thread went unacknowledged, then the thread resolved in that same direction. What would an ethical bystander do?

options.text: Name the source in the thread — "this is what he said above" — publicly, in the moment
options.note: Four seconds of typing. It costs the bystander nothing and it's the only thing that actually puts his name back on it.

options.text: React to or reply to the original message so it stops being invisible
options.note: Even lower effort. A thread with one reply reads completely differently from a thread with none.

options.text: In the sync, notice that Ellie's question was his answer and say so
options.note: Same pattern twice in one day, in two rooms. Somebody in that meeting had heard it before.

options.text: Privately message him to say it was unfair
options.note: Kind, and it changes nothing that happened in public. It also quietly makes him responsible for what to do next.

options.text: Say nothing, since the right outcome was reached anyway
options.note: The outcome was reached. The credit went somewhere else, and next time the room has slightly less reason to listen to him.

options.text: Report the thread to a manager
options.note: Enormous machinery for a Slack thread, and it takes it out of his hands. Delia already hasn't got time to adjudicate one report.

question: He tells a colleague he thinks his work was taken, but admits he can't prove it. What is a trauma-informed response?

options.text: Believe him without requiring proof first
options.note: He has already spent a day being disbelieved by someone holding the only evidence. Starting from belief is the entire difference between support and a second interrogation.

options.text: Acknowledge that not knowing is its own harm
options.note: Naming the ambiguity as real is a relief. It stops him privately wondering whether the problem is that he's paranoid.

options.text: Ask what he wants to do rather than telling him
options.note: Every decision that day was made over his head. This is the one that doesn't have to be.

options.text: Advise him to escalate to HR immediately
options.note: With what? He has no earlier version. Sending him into a process he can't win takes the decision off him and hands him a loss.

options.text: Point out that Pauline probably didn't mean it, so it's best let go
options.note: Probably true, and it's an argument about intent when the thing he needs acknowledged is effect.

options.text: Offer to confront Pauline on his behalf
options.note: Reads as solidarity. It's still someone else deciding what happens to him, and he's the one who works next to Pauline tomorrow.
